children.text: The seat of the Archdiocese of Manila stands on Plaza Roma in Intramuros; after fires, earthquakes and war destroyed it seven times, the current eighth building rose in
. Entry is free, and you can take in its stained glass and the largest pipe organ in the Philippines during Mass.

The official name of Manila Cathedral is the "Minor Basilica and Metropolitan Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception." It stands on Plaza Roma, the square at the heart of the walled city of Intramuros, and because it holds the cathedra of the Archbishop of Manila it is called the "mother church" of Philippine Catholicism. The Diocese of Manila was created by a papal bull of Pope Gregory XIII in
, and the parish church on this site formally became a cathedral on
December 21, 1581
. When Manila was raised to an archdiocese in
, the cathedral became the central church of Philippine Catholicism, a role it still holds today.
The cathedral's history is a record of eight rebuildings. The first cathedral, built of wood, bamboo and nipa palm, was lost in
when a fire that started at a governor's funeral in San Agustin Church swept through the city. The second, built of stone, fell in a powerful earthquake on the night of
December 31, 1600
, and the third collapsed in the earthquake of
. The fourth and fifth cathedrals were repaired and rebuilt again and again after typhoons and earthquakes until the earthquake of
September 16, 1852
caused heavy damage, and the sixth, opened in
, fell only five years later in the earthquake of
June 3, 1863
. The seventh, completed in
, lost its bell tower to an earthquake the following year but survived, only to be destroyed by bombing in the Battle of Manila in
, leaving just the facade and parts of the walls standing.
The present eighth cathedral was designed by architect Fernando Ocampo; its cornerstone was laid in
and it was consecrated on
December 7, 1958
. Echoing the old facade that survived as a ruin, it pairs a Neo-Romanesque front with Byzantine-style ornament, and its Latin-cross plan of about 3,000 m² makes lavish use of Italian marble. On
April 27, 1981

, Pope John Paul II granted it the title of minor basilica on his own initiative (motu proprio); it is the only church in the Philippines to become a basilica directly at a pope's own initiative. It closed in
February 2012
for seismic retrofitting and reopened on
April 9, 2014
, and on
January 16, 2015
Pope Francis celebrated Mass here.

With no entrance fee and Mass every day, it suits Catholic visitors as well as travelers interested in architecture, religious art and modern Philippine history. Its large air-conditioned interior is also a good place to escape the midday heat. The story of the whole walled city is covered in
Intramuros
, the Baroque church and its museum in
San Agustin Church
, and the fort and Rizal's footsteps in
Fort Santiago
; this guide focuses on the cathedral itself in depth.

Looking at the front from Plaza Roma, you can take in the three arched portals, the stone statues of saints, the round rose window and the clock tower on the left all at once. The semicircular wall (tympanum) above the central portal bears a Latin inscription meaning "To your Immaculate Heart we entrust and consecrate ourselves," and the bronze doors below show scenes from the cathedral's history of destruction and rebuilding in a series of relief panels.

Most of the 134 stained-glass windows around the church were designed by Filipino artist Galo Ocampo and depict scenes from Christian history and the saints, especially the life of the Virgin Mary. In the late afternoon, light filtering through the colored glass spills across the columns and marble floor, and the interior is at its most beautiful.

blocks.title: The largest pipe organ in the Philippines

children.text: The organ in the choir loft above the entrance was built in
by the Dutch organ builder Pels & Zoon; with four manuals and more than 5,000 pipes, it is the largest pipe organ in the Philippines. A major restoration was completed in
, and you can hear it fill the whole church during Sunday Mass or organ concerts.

blocks.title: The Immaculate Conception and the altar

children.text: Between the green marble columns at the back of the sanctuary stands the statue of the Immaculate Conception, the cathedral's patroness, and in front of it are the archbishop's chair and pulpit made of Italian marble. From the ceiling hang the red cardinal's hats (galeros) of Rufino Santos, the first Filipino cardinal, and Cardinal Jaime Sin, famous for "People Power."

Beneath the main altar is a crypt dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows, where Archbishop Michael O'Doherty, Gabriel Reyes, the first Filipino archbishop, Cardinal Rufino Santos and Cardinal Jaime Sin are laid to rest. It is normally closed to the public and opens only on special occasions such as the Independence Day open house on
, so check the cathedral's announcements.

The dome covered in green copper and the clock tower to the left of the facade are landmarks visible from all over the walled city. Inside, stand at the crossing beneath the dome and look up; outside, try framing the dome and the tower together from the Palacio del Gobernador on the west side of the square or from the road toward Fort Santiago.
Before it is a sight, it is a working cathedral. Mass is held on weekdays at
and
, and on Sundays at
and
; even if you are not Catholic, you can sit quietly in the back pews and listen to the hymns and the organ.
Plaza Roma, the square in front of the cathedral, was Manila's central square, known as the Plaza Mayor in Spanish times. In the middle stand a statue and fountain erected in

in honor of the Spanish king Charles IV, who sent the first smallpox vaccine to the Philippines, and the square is framed by the Palacio del Gobernador to the west and the Ayuntamiento building to the east. Every year on the
first Sunday of December
, the Grand Marian Procession is held around this square.
Attend the morning Mass if you wish. You can enjoy the sound of the organ from the choir loft together with the early-morning light through the stained glass.
From Plaza Roma, look at the facade and the bell tower, then take a close look at the tympanum inscription and the bronze door reliefs on the central portal.
Walk along the nave inside the church, taking in the side chapels, the crossing beneath the dome, and the statue of the Virgin and the cardinals' hats in the sanctuary.
40 minutes to 1 hour
is usually enough.
Rest in the shade across the square, then walk along General Luna Street to San Agustin Church.
Finish your visit to the San Agustin Museum before it closes for lunch (
), then have lunch at a nearby restaurant.
Arrive 20 minutes before Mass to find a seat. Sunday mornings are crowded with worshippers, so it is best to come early.
Attend Mass and listen to the pipe organ and the choir. Mass lasts about
1 hour
Once Mass is over and the crowd thins, look around the front of the altar and the side chapels. The office is open only until
on Sundays, so hurry if you have questions.
After lunch, continue in the afternoon to Fort Santiago or the walkway on top of the walls.

Fort Santiago

10 minutes

5–10 minutes
down to

so that your route never doubles back. On Mondays and holidays, when visiting the cathedral is difficult, reverse the order: start with the fort and a walk on the walls, and see the cathedral mainly from the outside and the square.
From near LRT Line 1 Carriedo station, a Pier-bound jeepney drops you near Plaza Roma in front of the cathedral in
10–15 minutes

There is parking around the cathedral, but it fills up quickly during Masses and weddings. The Intramuros Administration parking lots charge a flat
, so it is easier to park there and walk.
Take the free Pasig River Ferry run by the MMDA, get off at Escolta station and cross Jones Bridge; you reach the walls in
10–15 minutes
on foot, and the cathedral a few minutes after that. You need to show ID when boarding, and service stops for maintenance or when the river is high, so check the MMDA's announcements.
Plaza Roma in front of the cathedral is the starting point for transport inside the walls. The electric tricycle (e-trike) costs
per person on its fixed route, and a free electric tranvia (e-tranvia), on trial since
March 2026
, departs from the square twice a day (
and
3–4 PM
) on a loop of sights inside the walls. As it is a trial service, times may change.
The air-conditioned interior can be visited all year, but walking around the square and the walled city depends on the weather.
December–February
is relatively cool and dry and best for walking; in
March–May
midday temperatures climb to around
, so it is best to see the church in the morning and stay indoors at midday.
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and typhoons affect the area in
July–September
The cathedral's biggest feast is its patronal feast, the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary on
December 8
. Just before it, on the
first Sunday of December
, the Grand Marian Procession brings Marian images from across the country to Plaza Roma, and on
December 16–24
the pre-Christmas dawn Masses of Simbang Gabi fill the church with lights and people. During Holy Week (usually
late March–April
), Visita Iglesia pilgrims visiting seven churches crowd in. These days offer plenty to see, but general visits may be restricted.

There are few places to stay inside the walls, so most visitors stay in Ermita or Malate (about
10–15 minutes
by car, about
a night) or in Makati or BGC and visit from there. The Bayleaf Intramuros, inside the walls, costs about
a night and is within walking distance of the cathedral, which is convenient for early-morning Mass or the night views.

For lunch, the area around General Luna Street, which runs from the cathedral to San Agustin Church, is good for Filipino home cooking such as sinigang, adobo and lechon kawali. The long-running Barbara's is known for its dinner buffet with a traditional cultural show (about
per person). On hot afternoons, halo-halo or calamansi juice is a good way to cool down.
According to the cathedral's official website, office hours are
Tuesday to Saturday and

on Sunday, closed on Mondays and holidays. Travel guides also give these as visiting hours, so a Tuesday-to-Saturday morning visit is the safest bet. There is Mass on Mondays too, but do not expect visitor assistance. Check the latest announcements.
Mass is at
and
on weekdays,
on Saturdays, and
and
on Sundays. Do not walk around taking photos during Mass; look around after it ends.
This church hosts a great many weddings. The doors stay open even during ceremonies, but avoid the central aisle where the couple walks and the altar area, and move quietly along the side aisles.

If you would like a guided explanation, request a date and time in advance through the Tour Request form on the cathedral's official website. Unless you are in a group, following the highlights in this guide in order on your own is enough.
Late afternoon is best for photographing the stained glass, but the office opens only in the morning on Sundays, so choose a weekday afternoon. Do not use flash or tripods.
To hear the organ, aim for Sunday morning Mass or one of the organ concerts announced by the cathedral. Whether it is played varies from day to day.

To fit the whole facade in one frame, step back to the far side of Plaza Roma and shoot wide; the dome is best seen looking up from the side street on the right of the church or from the Palacio del Gobernador.
The cathedral interior alone takes
40 minutes to 1 hour
. The San Agustin Museum closes from
, so you can save time by seeing the cathedral first in the morning and heading straight to the museum.

Manila Cathedral is a working cathedral with a constant schedule of Masses, weddings, funerals and ordinations. During major ceremonies or feast days, general visits may be restricted or some areas closed off, so leave some slack in your schedule and check the latest announcements.

The Archdiocese of Manila asks visitors not to wear sleeveless tops, short skirts and shorts, low-cut clothing or caps inside churches. Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and bring a light layer if it is hot.
There may be touts and pickpockets on Plaza Roma and in front of the cathedral. Wear your bag in front, and agree clearly on the fare and duration before riding a horse carriage (kalesa) or pedicab.
The marble floor is slippery if you walk on it with wet shoes on rainy days. Watch your step on the stairs in front of the altar and at the thresholds of the side chapels.
There is little shade on the square, so there is a risk of heatstroke at midday. Drink plenty of water and take breaks inside the church.
Do not talk loudly on the phone or eat inside the church. Do not cut in front of people who are praying to take photos.
